input.question: Does every strict conditional independence model for discrete random variables have a Q-rational point? Here a strict conditional independence model is the intersection of the positive orthant with the constructible set of tables for which a specified collection of conditional independence statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | XK holds and all other such statements do not hold.

original_question: Does every strict conditional independence model for discrete random variables have a Q-rational point? Here a strict conditional independence model is the intersection of the positive orthant with the constructible set of tables for which a specified collection of conditional independence statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | XK holds and all other such statements do not hold.
rewritten_question: Let X1, X2, ..., Xn be discrete random variables with d1, d2, ..., dn possible states, and identify a joint distribution with a d1 × d2 × ··· × dn table of positive real numbers. For any conditional independence statement saying that Xi is independent of Xj given XK, the condition that this statement hold is expressed by the vanishing of certain 2 × 2 minors, so a chosen collection of such statements defines a conditional-independence variety in the space of tables. Fix one collection S of conditional independence statements. Its strict conditional-independence variety consists of those tables for which every statement in S holds and every other conditional independence statement of this form fails; the corresponding strict conditional-independence model is the intersection of that constructible set with the positive orthant. Must every nonempty strict conditional-independence model contain a table all of whose entries are rational numbers?

resolution.status_reason: The primary paper explicitly poses this as an open 'Bonus Problem' and says that, at the time of writing, 'we know next to nothing.' A bounded later-literature search using Crossref and the arXiv API with exact and near-exact query variants for strict conditional-independence models and Q-rational points did not uncover a credible later paper claiming a general resolution of this exact question.

paper_evidence.quote: We call such a variety a CI variety. It is the zero set of a large collection of 2×2-determinants. These constraints are well-known and listed explicitly in [12, §4.1] or [27, Proposition 8.1]. The corresponding strict CI variety is the set of tables for which the given CI statements hold but all other CI statements do not hold. Thus a strict CI variety is a constructible subset of (5.1) which is Zariski open in a CI variety.

The corresponding strict CI model is the intersection of the strict CI variety with the positive orthant. It consists of all positive d1×d2× · · · ×dn-tables that lie in a common equivalence class, where two tables are equivalent if precisely the same CI statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj |XK are valid (resp. not valid) for both tables. Bonus Problem: Does every strict CI model have a Q-rational point?

This charming problem was proposed by F. Matúš in [21, page 275]. It suggests that algebraic statistics has something to offer also for arithmetic geometers. One conceivable solution to the Bonus Problem might say that CI models with no rational points exist but that rational points always appear when the number of states grows large, that is, for d1, d2, . . . , dn ≫ 0. But that is pure speculation. At present we know next to nothing.
